what.title: What is neuroadaptation?
paragraphs: Neuroadaptation is the set of changes in the nervous system after repeated stimulation — including a substance. It can include functional changes and structural modifications of synaptic connections. It is not, by definition, the death of neurons or neurodegeneration.

It is plasticity: the same hardware can run a different programme. That idea connects with tolerance and physical dependence without making them synonyms or turning them into brain damage Soma can measure.

how.title: How does the nervous system change?
paragraphs: At the synapse, the amount of receptor in the membrane, its desensitisation, transmitter release or the strength of the connection (synaptic plasticity) can change. At the network scale, the tone of reward, stress and control circuits shifts.
None of that is a single switch of “more dopamine” or “less dopamine”. Reducing recovery to one messenger concentration is the error this sheet tries to avoid.
analogies: Think of a city that, faced with a new volume of traffic, changes traffic lights, diversions and drivers’ habits. That is network adaptation. It is not the same as demolishing buildings (neurodegeneration).

The analogy shows functional change versus loss of structure. It fails if it is translated as “the brain fully rewires in X days”, or as if every diversion undid itself at once when the extra traffic stopped.

kinds.title: Plasticity versus neurodegeneration
paragraphs: Neuroadaptation does not necessarily mean neuronal damage. Neurodegeneration is loss or injury of nerve cells. Neuroadaptation is mainly a change of function and, sometimes, of synapse architecture — how many there are, how they are organised — not the loss of neurons. Heavy chronic alcohol can, in some contexts, be associated with toxicity; that does not licence calling every adaptation to caffeine or nicotine “damage”.
The two ideas can coexist in the same person and still not be the same thing. Soma does not do neuroimaging or count neurons.

where.title: Reward, stress and control
paragraphs: Reward circuits (including the mesolimbic pathway) can become less sensitive to everyday rewards or more sensitive to cues for the substance. Stress circuits — amygdala, corticotropin-releasing factor systems, hormonal axis — can gain weight when the drug is missing. Control circuits — prefrontal cortex and its connections — take part in regulating impulses and habits.
This is a working map from the neurobiology of addiction, not a diagnosis by brain region. Not every change happens in every person or with every Soma substance.

substances.title: How it crosses Soma’s substances
paragraphs: Each substance pushes different doors — DAT, nicotinic receptors, CB1, GABA-A and NMDA, adenosine — and therefore writes different adaptations. Each messenger sheet already covers those mechanisms; the rule here is: there is no single “substance brain”.
Caffeine does not copy alcohol. Nicotine does not copy cocaine. Mixing them into one neuroadaptation story would be a map error.

connections.title: Links with tolerance, dependence and withdrawal
paragraphs: Neuroadaptation can contribute to tolerance (the target answers less, or the network compensates) and to physical dependence (the balance counts on the substance). Withdrawal is, in part, that adaptation without the drug.
Metabolism determines how much substance is there and for how long; it is not neuroadaptation. Emptying the plasma does not by itself reset the network’s traffic lights.

stopping.title: Reversible and persistent change
paragraphs: When use stops, some changes start to reverse; others may last longer. The pace is not uniform across regions, effects or people. There are no universal calendars of brain recovery this app can apply.
“The substance is gone” does not equal “the brain has returned to a catalogue snapshot”. Soma does not measure your plasticity.

caveats.title: What we know — and what to keep in perspective
paragraphs: Neuroadaptation is not neurodegeneration by default. Not all changes reverse at the same pace. There is no universal calendar and no single neurotransmitter concentration that summarises recovery. This sheet describes general mechanisms; it does not describe your brain.

what.title: What is the metabolism of a substance?
paragraphs: In pharmacology, metabolism — or biotransformation — is the set of reactions with which the body modifies a substance, often in the liver, to make elimination easier. It does not mean only “clearing” or “eliminating”: sometimes the metabolite is still active, or even more active than the original molecule.
Confusing metabolism with neuronal recovery is this sheet’s map error. Processing a molecule does not by itself undo nervous-system adaptations.

how.title: Absorption, distribution, transformation and elimination
paragraphs: The classic route is four steps (ADME). Absorption: the substance enters the bloodstream from the gut, the lung, a mucosa or another route. Distribution: it spreads through tissues, including the brain if it crosses barriers. Metabolism: enzymes transform it. Elimination: it is excreted, mainly in urine or, in some cases, in air or faeces.

Half-life — the time in which plasma concentration falls by half, when the model allows it — is not the same as duration of effect. Effect also depends on which receptors remain occupied, on active metabolites, and on the lag between concentration and response.
analogies: Think of a warehouse that receives a parcel (absorption), places it on different shelves (distribution), takes it apart or relabels it (metabolism) and ships it out (elimination). A relabel can leave an object that is still useful (active metabolite).
The analogy shows a procedure, not a cure. It fails if it is translated as “when the warehouse is empty, the city has already undone every diversion”, or as a calculator for toxicology tests.

kinds.title: Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics
paragraphs: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does with the substance (ADME). Pharmacodynamics describes what the substance does at its targets (receptors, enzymes, channels). Tolerance and dependence live mainly in pharmacodynamics and neuroadaptation, although an enzyme change (pharmacokinetics) can contribute to tolerance.
Mixing the two is saying that “it has already been cleared” equals “there is no residual effect and no adaptation”. It does not.

where.title: Liver, kidneys and other tissues
paragraphs: The liver holds many cytochrome P450 enzymes — CYP names that enzyme family — and other routes (alcohol dehydrogenase, esterases). The kidneys filter and excrete metabolites. There is also metabolism in gut, lung and plasma, depending on the molecule.
Genetics, age, other drugs, smoking or liver disease change those routes. That is why there is no individual clock Soma can calculate.

substances.title: Soma’s five substances
paragraphs: Alcohol. It is oxidised mainly by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase; with chronic use the CYP2E1 route can gain weight. It is not cleared like a catecholamine. In certain concentration ranges some metabolic routes saturate and kinetics can look closer to a steadier rate; that is not a universal pattern and not a personal clock. That does not licence calculating “how many hours you have left” in this app.

Nicotine. It is largely transformed into cotinine, with a prominent role for CYP2A6. Caffeine. CYP1A2 is the classic route; smoking can induce it and speed clearance in many people. Cocaine. It has several metabolic routes: hydrolytic pathways — plasma and liver esterases that generate metabolites such as benzoylecgonine — and other enzymatic transformations. That is not Soma’s verdict on a test. Cannabis (THC). It is hydroxylated to an 11-OH metabolite that is also active, then to carboxylic acids that can be detectable longer than the felt effect.
Five doors in, five procedures. There is no single “drug half-life”.

connections.title: Metabolism, exposure and recovery
paragraphs: Metabolism determines part of exposure: how much substance arrives, how long it lasts in plasma, whether there is an active metabolite. It does not by itself explain tolerance, dependence or circuit recovery.
Clearing a substance does not mean every physiological adaptation has gone. Neuroadaptation keeps its own time.

stopping.title: When the substance is no longer there
paragraphs: When concentration falls, acute effects fade before many adaptations. Detectable metabolites, disrupted sleep or withdrawal can remain, depending on the substance, without proving a catalogue number of “clean” days.

This sheet does not offer individual clearance calculations or guarantees of absence on toxicology tests. A test depends on thresholds, matrices (urine, blood, hair) and the pattern of use; Soma does not interpret your labs.

caveats.title: What we know — and what to keep in perspective
paragraphs: Metabolism is not only elimination. Half-life is not duration of effect. Emptying the plasma does not reset the nervous system. There is no detox calculator and no test guarantee here. This sheet describes general procedures; it does not describe your liver or your brain.
